passages.t: ‘Much in every way’: God stays faithful
passages.happening:
After chapter 2, a Jewish listener might ask: then what was the point of being God's people? Paul puts the question himself: “What, then, is the advantage of being a Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision?” (verse 1).

His answer: “Much in every way. First of all, they have been entrusted with the very words of God” (verse 2).

Then a harder question. “What if some did not have faith? Will their lack of faith nullify God’s faithfulness?” (verse 3). “Certainly not! Let God be true and every man a liar” (verse 4).

The questions keep coming. If our wrong shows up God's rightness, is God unfair to punish us (verse 5)? “Certainly not! In that case, how could God judge the world?” (verse 6). If my lie makes God's truth shine brighter, why am I still judged as a sinner (verse 7)? Why not say, as some slander Paul for saying, “Let us do evil that good may result”? Paul's reply is short: such people deserve their condemnation (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
‘The very words of God’ is the BSB's phrase. Older English Bibles say ‘the oracles of God’. It means the Scriptures: the promises, the law and the prophets that God gave to Israel. Every Gentile believer in Rome who read the Bible was reading Israel's book. That is a great advantage, and Paul never takes it back.

The question in verse 3 is the real question of the whole letter. If most of Israel has not believed in Jesus, has God failed? Paul gives a short answer here, ‘Certainly not’, and the long answer in chapters 9 to 11.

‘Certainly not’ is a strong Greek expression, mē genoito, roughly ‘may it never be’. Paul uses it again and again in Romans to throw out a wrong conclusion. Older Bibles translate it ‘God forbid’.

Verse 8 shows something about Paul's life. People were already twisting his message. If God saves sinners freely, they said, Paul must be teaching that sin does not matter, or even that sin is useful. He will answer that properly in chapter 6. Here he simply refuses it.
passages.ot:
Verse 4 quotes Psalm 51, David's prayer after his sin with Bathsheba. David confesses, “Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight, so that You may be proved right when You speak and blameless when You judge” (Psalm 51:4). Paul follows the Greek translation, which ends ‘victorious when You judge’. David's point, and Paul's, is that when a sinner confesses, God is shown to be in the right.

‘Let God be true and every man a liar’ echoes another psalm: “All men are liars” (Psalm 116:11).

The Scriptures entrusted to Israel include Moses's words: “what nation is great enough to have righteous statutes and ordinances like this entire law I set before you today?” (Deuteronomy 4:8).
passages.hard: If our sin makes God's goodness shine, why should God judge it? Paul treats this as a trick of logic, and he will not play. A judge does not become unjust because a criminal's guilt makes his fairness obvious. And the idea that we might do evil so that good may come is not a clever reading of grace; Paul calls it slander. Grace does not make sin useful. It makes forgiveness possible. Chapter 6 gives his full answer.
passages.asks: Paul says the Jewish people were given a great gift: the words of God. So were you, if you hold a Bible. Ask how you treat that gift. And notice how Paul answers clever excuses for sin: he does not argue long. Ask what excuses you have built for the wrong you would like to keep.

passages.happening:
“What then? Are we any better? Not at all” (verse 9). Paul has shown that Jews and Greeks alike are “all under sin” (verse 9).

Then he proves it from Scripture, with a chain of quotations (verses 10-18). “There is no one righteous, not even one. There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God” (verses 10-11). All have turned away and become worthless; no one does good, not one (verse 12). “Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit” (verse 13). “The venom of vipers is on their lips” (verse 13). “Their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness” (verse 14). “Their feet are swift to shed blood” (verse 15); ruin and misery lie in their wake, and the way of peace they have not known (verses 16-17). “There is no fear of God before their eyes” (verse 18).

What the law says, it says to those under the law, “so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God” (verse 19). “Therefore no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law. For the law merely brings awareness of sin” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
A chain of Bible quotations like this was a known way of making a case: line after line of Scripture, laid side by side. Jewish hearers would know many of these lines by heart from the Psalms.

Notice how the chain moves through the body. It starts with the whole person, then goes to the throat, the tongue, the lips, the mouth, the feet and finally the eyes. Every part of life is covered. Most of the sins named are sins of speech.

Verse 19 matters. The law was given to Israel. So when the Scriptures say ‘no one is righteous’, they are not only describing pagans far away. They are speaking to the people who had the law. That is why ‘every mouth’ is silenced, Jewish and Gentile. The trial that began in 1:18 ends here. Nobody has anything left to say in their own defence.

‘Works of the law’ in verse 20 is a phrase Christians read in more than one way. The book page sets out the two main readings: deeds done to earn standing with God, or the practices, like circumcision, that marked Jews off from others.

‘The law merely brings awareness of sin’. The law shows what is wrong, like a mirror that shows the dirt on a face. A mirror cannot wash the face.
passages.ot:
Paul gathers his chain from the Psalms and Isaiah. Here is each one in its own place.

Two of the lines come from Psalm 14, repeated in Psalm 53: “There is no one who does good” (Psalm 14:1) and “All have turned away, they have together become corrupt” (Psalm 14:3). There ‘the fool’ says in his heart that there is no God, and God looks down to see if any seek him. Ecclesiastes says the same: “Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins” (Ecclesiastes 7:20).

“Their throats are open graves; their tongues practice deceit” is from Psalm 5:9, a prayer against lying enemies. “The venom of vipers is on their lips” is from Psalm 140:3, a prayer for rescue from violent men. The mouth “full of cursing” is from Psalm 10:7, about the wicked who hunt the poor.

The feet ‘swift to shed blood’ and ‘the way of peace they have not known’ are from Isaiah 59:7-8, where the prophet describes Jerusalem's own injustice. The chain ends with Psalm 36: “There is no fear of God before his eyes” (Psalm 36:1).

Verse 20 echoes David's prayer: “for no one alive is righteous before You” (Psalm 143:2). Many of these psalms first described the wicked as other people. Paul's point is that, in God's sight, the lines describe all of us.
passages.hard: Does Paul mean that no one ever does anything good? He has already said that Gentiles sometimes do what the law requires (2:14). His point here is about standing before God: no one is righteous before him on their own record. Christians differ on how deeply sin reaches. The Reformed tradition teaches that sin touches every part of a person, mind, will and desires, though not that people are as bad as they could be. Catholic and Orthodox teaching speaks of human nature as wounded and weakened by sin, but not wholly corrupted. All agree with Paul's verdict: every mouth is silenced, and no one can be set right with God by their own deeds.
passages.asks: Most of Paul's list is about the mouth: deceit, poison, cursing, bitterness. Ask what your words this week would say about your heart. Then let verse 19 do its work. Paul wants every mouth stopped, not to crush people, but so that they stop defending themselves and are ready to hear what comes next.

passages.t: ‘But now’: righteousness from God, and the cross
passages.happening:
Here is the turning point of the letter. “But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed, as attested by the Law and the Prophets” (verse 21).

“And this righteousness from God comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no distinction” (verse 22), “for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (verse 23), “and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (verse 24).

“God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood, in order to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand” (verse 25).

“He did this to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
‘But now’. After two and a half chapters of the courtroom, with every mouth silenced, the door opens. Paul marks it with two short words.

He uses three pictures from three places that every hearer knew.

The law court: ‘justified’ means declared in the right by a judge. All have sinned, Paul says, and all who believe are justified. The ground is level. ‘There is no distinction.’

The slave market: ‘redemption’ was the word for paying a price to set a slave or a prisoner free. Many in the Roman house churches were slaves or freed slaves. They knew what it meant to be bought out.

The temple: ‘the atoning sacrifice’ is the place and means where sin is dealt with and God meets his people. The note below explains the word.

‘Freely’ means as a gift, for nothing. ‘By His grace’ means out of God's undeserved kindness.

‘Fall short of the glory of God’. In chapter 1 people exchanged God's glory for images (1:23). Human beings were made to reflect God's glory, and sin has left them short of it.

Verse 25 answers a question. In the past God ‘passed over’ sins. He was patient, and did not punish as sin deserved. But a judge who simply lets the guilty go is not just. The cross shows that God never took sin lightly. In it he is both ‘just’, dealing with sin truly, and the one who ‘justifies’, setting the guilty right.

‘Faith in Jesus Christ’ (verse 22) can also be translated ‘the faithfulness of Jesus Christ’. The book page sets out both readings.
passages.ot:
Paul says this righteousness was ‘attested by the Law and the Prophets’. He means passages like Abraham's faith, “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6), which he takes up in chapter 4, and Habakkuk 2:4, which he quoted in 1:17.

Redemption was God's word for the exodus: “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment” (Exodus 6:6).

The word behind ‘atoning sacrifice’ is the Greek Old Testament's word for the mercy seat, the gold cover on the ark of the covenant. God told Moses, “I will meet with you there above the mercy seat” (Exodus 25:22). Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, the high priest sprinkled blood “on the east side of the mercy seat” (Leviticus 16:14) to make atonement for the people. Hebrews uses the same word for “the mercy seat” (Hebrews 9:5).

Isaiah's servant bears the sins of others: “He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5), and “My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities” (Isaiah 53:11).
passages.hard:
What does ‘atoning sacrifice’ mean in verse 25, and what did the cross do? The Greek word is hilastērion. The BSB has ‘the atoning sacrifice’, with ‘propitiation’ in its footnote. Scholars read it in three main ways. Propitiation means turning away God's just anger against sin; its defenders point to 1:18, where Paul began with the wrath of God. Expiation means wiping away sin itself; C. H. Dodd argued for it in 1935, and Leon Morris answered in 1955 for propitiation. Mercy seat follows the Greek Old Testament: God has set Christ out in public as the place where sin is dealt with and God meets his people. Many readers think more than one is in view.

Christians also describe in different ways what the cross achieved. Penal substitution, taught especially in Reformation churches, holds that Christ bore the penalty of sin in the place of sinners. The view called Christus Victor, named in a book of 1930 by the Swedish theologian Gustaf Aulén, stresses Christ's victory over sin, death and the devil, and is held to be the view of many early church writers. Others stress Christ's obedience offered to the Father, or the cross as the great showing of God's love that changes those who see it. Many Christians hold these pictures together, while others put one at the centre. Some object that punishing an innocent person is unjust; defenders reply that the one who bears it is not a third party but God himself in the Son, giving himself freely.

These notes do not choose between them. The Nicene Creed, shared by the churches, confesses that the Son came down ‘for us men and for our salvation’. Every reading stands on that ground.
passages.asks: ‘There is no distinction’: all have sinned, and all who believe are justified freely. Ask whether you secretly think you are an exception, either too good to need this or too bad to receive it. Then sit with verse 26. God did not wink at your sin. He dealt with it, at the cost of his Son, and freely sets you right.

passages.t: No boasting, one God, the law upheld
passages.happening:
“Where, then, is boasting? It is excluded” (verse 27). On what principle? Works? “No, but on that of faith” (verse 27). “For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (verse 28).

Then Paul asks, “Is God the God of Jews only? Is He not the God of Gentiles too? Yes, of Gentiles too” (verse 29), “since there is only one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith” (verse 30).

Last question: “Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith? Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Boasting, in Paul's world, was a normal part of public life. People boasted of their family, their city, their learning, their honours. Paul says that before God all of that is shut out. If you are set right with God as a gift, there is nothing left to be proud of.

Verse 29 shows that Paul's argument is not only about one person and God. It is about Jews and Gentiles in the house churches of Rome. If everyone is justified the same way, by faith, then no one can look down on another believer. One God means one people.

‘Through that same faith’. Jew and Gentile come in by the same door.

Paul's critics said his gospel made the law worthless. He says the reverse. How faith ‘upholds the law’ he will begin to show at once, in chapter 4, where he shows from the law itself, the book of Genesis, that Abraham was set right with God by faith.
passages.ot:
Verse 30 rests on Israel's great confession, recited in Jewish prayer: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). If there is one God, Paul says, he is the God of every nation, and he sets every nation right in the same way.

The prophets looked for the day when the nations would worship Israel's God: “Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:22).

The warning against boasting is old too. Jeremiah says, “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom” (Jeremiah 9:23), and, “But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me” (Jeremiah 9:24).
passages.hard: If people are justified apart from works of the law, does the law still matter? Paul says faith ‘upholds’ it, and readers explain that in a few ways. Some say the law's own witness is fulfilled: the law, in Genesis, already taught that Abraham was justified by faith (chapter 4). Some say the Spirit enables believers to fulfil what the law truly requires (8:4). Others say the law's moral demand still stands as a guide for life, though not as a way to earn standing with God. These readings can stand together. What Paul rules out is that faith makes the law worthless.
passages.asks: Boasting is excluded. Ask what you are quietly proud of before God: your background, your church, your knowledge, your clean record. Then ask how you treat believers who came to faith by a different road. If God is the God of all, and justifies all the same way, there is no room to look down on anyone.
